newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Southeast Asian currencies calmer but still fragile.
newsitem.headline: Southeast Asian currencies calmer but still fragile.

text.p: Southeast Asian currencies remained weak but relatively subdued on Wednesday as players paused to catch their breath after days of frenzy.
In Indonesia and Malaysia, the prospect of a holiday on Thursday helped keep a bid tone to the dollar as the market remained cautious of possible volatility.
But a Japanese bank dealer said spreads were narrowing, suggesting improved confidence in the market.

"There is good demand from both local and foreign side but supply is also sufficient. People don't want to be caught too long or too short if other markets turn naughty on Thursday," another dealer said.
Jakarta dealers said the rupiah was also depressed by ample money market liquidity.
Spot rupiah was at 2,457.0/58.0 at 0400 GMT against an opening 2,453 and a New York close at 2,458/59.
The Malaysian ringgit was confined to a narrow range as operators took profit after the dollar's failure to breach the 2.5700 level, where the central bank was believed to have intervened.
"U.S. hedge funds were seen taking profit at 2.5650 this morning," a European bank dealer in Kuala Lumpur said. "The market is long dollars and this will slow down its rise."
The ringgit was at 2.5630/40 to the dollar at 0400 GMT against its Kuala Lumpur close at 2.5580/10 on Tuesday.
"The dollar is coming back offered because the market was speculatively long for the last few days. But nobody has a clue what to do up here," a U.S. bank dealer in Singapore said.
He said dollar/ringgit remained an attractive buy below the 2.55 level but levels above 2.57 should inspire caution.
Dealers said the ringgit's undertone remained bearish due to a perceived change in stance by Malaysian authorities.
Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim said on Tuesday Malaysia would allow its exchange rate to be determined by market forces and that it did not favour a high interest rate regime.
Anwar's comments baffled the market after Bank Negara governor Ahmad Mohamed Don said last week that interest rates would stay high to curb speculation in the ringgit.
The Thai baht held above the 30 level against the dollar despite offshore attempts to push it down, prompting speculation of intervention by the Bank of Thailand (BOT).
Dealers said the BOT might have stepped in to prop up the baht as it climbed from around 30.500/30.750 per dollar to 29.900/30.200 and to 29.350-29.450 later.
It was quoted at 29.850/30.000 at 0400 GMT offshore and 30.000/30.100 onshore.
Singapore dealers said the baht had come under pressure on vague rumours that BOT governor Rerngchai Marakanond was to resign, but most attached little credence to the idea.

"The political bodies in Thailand would have more sense than to allow such a thing to happen. The fact that it originated offshore and onshore is oblivious to it reinforces the idea that it could be a speculative ploy," the U.S. bank dealer said.

"Anything above 30 baht is going to be carefully watched by the BOT. Now that the currency's a free float, it's important for them to send a signal that they can control it if they want to," he added.
The baht has fallen about 15 percent since the BOT switched to a managed float on July 2 from the previous system of pegging the baht to a basket of currencies.
The Philippine peso continued to weaken after last week's move to allow it to trade in a wider band, seen as a de facto devaluation.
Traders said the central bank had sold dollars at 29 pesos in early trade, helping the currency stabilise somewhat. It was at 28.900/29.000 at 0400 GMT against a previous close at 29.
